title: How to Write a Winning Public Sector Bid
author_bio: Philip has over 24 years of recruitment experience and has provided specialist bid, proposal and tender writing services for the last 14 years, across frameworks including Crown Commercial Service, Workforce Alliance and HTE.
excerpt: After fourteen years writing and reviewing tenders, the same handful of things separate a bid that scores well from one that quietly comes last, and almost none of it has to do with how good the business actually is.
body:
I've read more losing bids than winning ones. That's not a boast, it's just the nature of the job. After fourteen years writing tenders and reviewing other people's, you start to notice the same handful of things separating a bid that scores well from one that quietly comes last, and almost none of it has to do with how good the business actually is.

Most of the companies I've worked with over the years were perfectly capable of delivering the contract. Some of them were better than the supplier who eventually won. What they weren't always good at was writing a document that proved it to someone who has never met them and never will.

Start with the scoring matrix, not the question

Every tender comes with a breakdown of how marks are awarded, and most people skim it once and then go straight to writing. Read it properly first. If quality is worth 70 percent and price is worth 30, that tells you where your effort needs to go. If a single question is worth 15 percent of the entire submission, that question deserves more than a paragraph lifted from last year's bid.

I still see businesses write a beautifully polished answer to a question nobody asked, because it's the answer they're proud of, not the one the buyer wants. The evaluator isn't grading your company. They're grading how precisely your answer matches their mark scheme. Those are not the same exercise.

Answer the actual question

This sounds obvious until you read a few hundred submissions. A buyer asks how you'll manage staff turnover on a contract and gets back three paragraphs about the company's general training philosophy. It's not wrong information, it's just not an answer. If the question has three parts, answer all three, in order, and make it easy for the evaluator to find each one.

A trick that helps more than people expect: lift the question's own language back into your answer. If they ask about "continuity of service during staff absence," use that exact phrase early in your response. Evaluators are often scoring dozens of submissions against a checklist, and a response that visibly tracks the question gets read more carefully than one that makes them hunt for the relevant bit.

Evidence beats confidence

"We have a highly experienced team" tells the evaluator nothing they can score. "Our account managers have an average of nine years in public sector recruitment, and we retained 94 percent of placed staff on our last NHS framework contract" tells them something specific, checkable, and comparable to the next supplier's answer.

If you don't have a strong number for something, say so honestly and explain what you do instead. A specific, modest claim backed by evidence will always outscore a vague, impressive sounding one. Evaluators have seen enough generic bids to be suspicious of confidence that isn't backed up.

Build one consistent story, not twelve separate answers

The strongest bids read like they were written by one person with one clear argument for why this supplier is the right choice, even when six different people contributed sections. Decide early what your two or three win themes are, the real reasons you're a good fit for this specific contract, and make sure they show up consistently across the document rather than being buried in one answer and absent from the rest.

Compliance is how you lose without ever being scored

Every year I see a genuinely strong submission disqualified for something that had nothing to do with the quality of the writing. A missing attachment. A word count ignored. A document uploaded to the wrong portal section five minutes after the deadline. None of that gets you marked down, it gets you removed from consideration entirely, and no amount of good writing afterward changes that.

Build in time at the end specifically for a compliance check against the instructions document, done by someone who hasn't been staring at the bid for two weeks and has gone slightly blind to it.

The businesses that win aren't always the best ones

They're the ones who treated the written response as seriously as the service they're actually offering. That's the part I'd want any business new to tendering to take away from this. The work you do and the bid you write are two different disciplines, and getting good at the second one is entirely learnable, it just takes someone willing to read the scoring criteria properly and resist the urge to write the answer they'd rather give.

If you want a second pair of eyes on a live tender before you submit it, that's exactly what we're here for.

title: A Guide to G-Cloud 14 for IT Consultancies
author_bio: James leads business development and bid management at Hawkeye Solutions, with particular success across G-Cloud and Digital Outcomes and Specialists frameworks, helping IT consultancies win public sector contracts.
excerpt: Getting onto G-Cloud is the easy part. Winning work through it is where most IT consultancies either get it right, or waste a listing that never earns them a single call-off.
body:
Every few months someone asks me the same question: should we get onto G-Cloud? The honest answer is usually yes, but with a caveat nobody tells you upfront, which is that getting on the framework is the easy part. Winning work through it is where most IT consultancies either get it right or waste a listing that never earns them a single call-off.

What G-Cloud actually is

G-Cloud is a Crown Commercial Service framework that lets public sector buyers, central government, NHS trusts, local authorities, buy cloud services without running a full open tender for every purchase. Instead, approved suppliers list their services on the Digital Marketplace, and buyers either browse and award directly for smaller purchases or run a short mini-competition between a handful of suppliers for bigger ones.

It renews roughly every two years. G-Cloud 14 is the current iteration, and if you're reading this after a new version has launched, the structure and the advice below will still largely hold, the framework gets refreshed more than it gets reinvented.

The three lots, in plain terms

G-Cloud splits into three categories, and most consultancies only genuinely belong in one or two of them.

  • Lot 1, Cloud Hosting. Infrastructure and platform services: compute, storage, hosting environments. If you're a hosting or infrastructure provider, this is you.
  • Lot 2, Cloud Software. Software as a service, applications buyers can procure directly. This is the most competitive lot by volume of listings.
  • Lot 3, Cloud Support. The one most IT consultancies actually belong in: implementation, migration, ongoing support, and specialist cloud services. If you help organisations plan, build or run cloud systems rather than selling the infrastructure itself, this is your lot.

Getting this right matters because buyers search by lot and by category tags within it. List yourself under the wrong one and you're invisible to the people actually looking for what you do.

Applying isn't a tender, but treat it like one anyway

The application window is short, usually a few weeks, and it opens roughly every two years rather than on demand. You'll need to evidence your company's financial standing, provide service descriptions for everything you're listing, and set your pricing. None of it is scored competitively in the way a normal tender is: if you meet the standard, you're in. But the quality of what you write at this stage determines whether anyone finds you once you are.

Write your service descriptions the way you'd write marketing copy aimed at a time-pressed procurement officer, not the way you'd write an internal capability document. Specific, plain, and focused on the outcome a buyer gets, not the technology stack you're proud of.

Where the real competition happens

Being on G-Cloud gets you a listing. It doesn't get you work. Buyers find suppliers two ways: direct award, where they search the marketplace and pick a supplier whose listing answers their need clearly enough to award without further competition, and mini-competitions, where a shortlist of suppliers is invited to respond to a short brief, often with a tight turnaround of a week or two.

The direct award route rewards clarity. A listing that's vague about what you actually do, or buried in jargon, simply won't come up in the searches that matter. The mini-competition route rewards speed and preparation: have case studies, pricing structures and reference material ready to go before the invitation lands, because a two-week turnaround doesn't leave room to start from scratch.

The mistakes I see most often

Consultancies list themselves once and never touch it again. Service descriptions written two years ago, pricing that's drifted out of date, no case studies added even after winning real contracts through the framework. A stale listing looks exactly like an inactive supplier to a buyer browsing the marketplace, and they move on to the next one.

The other common mistake is pricing too cautiously out of fear of looking expensive, then discovering the day rate doesn't cover the actual cost of delivery once a mini-competition is won. Price for the work you'd actually want to do, not the lowest number that might win something.

Why it's worth doing properly

We've helped IT consultancies through both the application and the call-off stages, and the pattern holds every time: the businesses that treat their G-Cloud presence as an ongoing piece of marketing, kept current and specific, consistently outperform the ones who listed themselves once and hoped. If you're applying for the first time, or your listing has gone quiet, it's worth a proper look before the next renewal window closes.

title: A Guide to RM6277 for Recruitment Agencies
author_bio: Philip has over 24 years of recruitment experience and has provided specialist bid, proposal and tender writing services for the last 14 years, across frameworks including Crown Commercial Service, Workforce Alliance and HTE.
excerpt: Ask ten recruitment agencies which public sector framework actually matters and most will say RM6277 before anything else. Here's what it covers, and where most agencies lose ground once they're on it.
body:
Ask ten recruitment agencies which public sector framework actually matters and most of them will say RM6277 before anything else. It's the Crown Commercial Service's Non-Clinical Staffing framework, and if you supply temporary or permanent staff into the NHS or wider public sector, getting onto it properly is usually worth more than any single tender you could chase on the open market.

What RM6277 actually covers

RM6277 is the current Crown Commercial Service agreement for sourcing non-clinical staff: admin, estates, corporate, facilities and operational roles, as distinct from the clinical and nursing frameworks that sit alongside it. NHS trusts and a wide range of public bodies use it to procure both temporary and permanent staffing without running a full open tender for every requirement.

Like most CCS frameworks, it's structured into lots, typically split by role category and region, and suppliers are awarded onto the specific lots that match what they actually recruit for. Being on the framework doesn't mean you're eligible for every vacancy a trust posts, only the lots you successfully applied against, so the application stage is where you decide your own ceiling for years to come.

Getting onto it versus winning through it

Same lesson as every framework I've worked on: the application and the ongoing competition for work are two entirely different exercises. Applying is a one-off event, usually with a fixed window that doesn't reopen for a long time once it closes. Winning call-offs happens continuously, through direct award for smaller or more standard requirements and mini-competition for larger or more complex ones, and that's where most of the real value sits over the life of the framework.

Agencies that treat the application as the finish line usually plateau. The ones that treat it as the starting gun, and build a genuine process for responding fast and well to call-offs, are the ones still winning three years in.

What buyers are actually scoring

Mini-competition responses on RM6277 get evaluated the same way any public sector tender does: against a published scoring matrix, usually weighted toward quality and delivery capability as much as rate. Buyers want evidence you can actually fill the roles you're bidding to supply, not just a lower day rate than the next agency on the lot. Fill rates, time to shortlist, candidate retention and your track record on comparable public sector placements all carry real weight, and vague claims about "a strong candidate network" score badly against an evaluator who has read the same sentence from six other suppliers that week.

Where agencies lose ground

Three things I see repeatedly. First, treating every mini-competition invitation the same regardless of fit, which burns capacity on opportunities you were never going to win and makes your response quality slip on the ones you should have focused on. Second, letting compliance evidence go stale: insurance certificates, right-to-work processes, safeguarding policies, all of which get checked and all of which can quietly disqualify a strong response if they've lapsed. Third, not updating your own capability evidence as your business grows, so a response written against your capacity from two years ago undersells what you can actually deliver now.

Is it worth the effort to apply

If a meaningful share of your current or target client base is NHS or wider public sector, yes, almost without exception. The application itself takes real work: proper evidence of financial standing, service descriptions written the way an evaluator reads rather than the way you'd pitch a private client, and a realistic view of which lots you can actually resource. But the agencies we've supported onto RM6277 and similar frameworks consistently describe it as the single biggest unlock in their public sector pipeline, not because it guarantees work, but because it's the gate you have to be through before any of the real competition even starts.

If you're weighing up whether to apply, or you're already on the framework and want a second opinion on why your mini-competition win rate isn't where it should be, that's exactly the conversation we have with clients every week.
